drills.q: Design a greedy algorithm for maximum non-overlapping intervals and state its complexity.
drills.a: Sort intervals by finish time, O(n log n); greedily take any interval that doesn't overlap the last taken one, O(n) scan.

drills.q: Prove the interval-scheduling greedy choice is optimal using an exchange argument.
drills.a: If OPT's first interval finishes later than greedy's earliest-finishing pick, swap it in. Feasibility holds since greedy's pick finishes no later, so it can't conflict with anything the swapped-out interval didn't already conflict with; count is unchanged. Induct on the remainder to show greedy matches an optimal solution everywhere.

drills.q: Construct a concrete counterexample showing greedy-by-value/weight-ratio fails on 0/1 knapsack.
drills.a: Capacity 10; items (w=6,v=12, ratio 2.0), (w=5,v=9, ratio 1.8), (w=5,v=9, ratio 1.8). Greedy takes the first item only (value 12, can't fit the rest). Optimal takes both weight-5 items (value 18).

drills.q: Given coin denominations {1,3,4} and amount 6, show greedy largest-first fails and give the DP complexity to solve it correctly in general.
drills.a: Greedy: 4+1+1 = 3 coins. Optimal: 3+3 = 2 coins. General correct algorithm is DP: O(amount * len(coins)) time, O(amount) space -- no greedy rule is safe without first proving the coin system is canonical.

drills.q: Prove no single per-item scoring function (value, weight, ratio, or combination) can make greedy correct for 0/1 knapsack in general.
drills.a: Construct two problem instances where the same fixed scoring-based ordering produces a correct answer on one and a wrong answer on the other -- because capacity constraints create combinatorial interactions between which subset of items fits, which no single per-item score can capture; this is exactly the exhaustive combination-checking that DP performs and greedy cannot.

drills.q: Explain why the 'minimum meeting rooms' problem cannot be solved with the same exchange argument used for 'maximum non-overlapping intervals,' even though both involve intervals.
drills.a: Maximum non-overlapping intervals is a selection-maximization problem (some intervals are rejected). Minimum rooms is a concurrent-overlap-counting problem (every interval must be scheduled, just possibly in different rooms) -- it requires a sweep over start/end events or a min-heap of active end times, not a sequential accept/reject greedy choice with a one-line exchange proof.
